current_definition: Having a pleasantly smooth, rich, and sweet sound that flows easily and is agreeable to listen to.
A formal speech delivered to an audience.
The quality of using very few words or taking very little time to express something; conciseness.
To bring up a sensitive or difficult subject for the first time in a conversation or discussion.
Logically connected and easy to follow; said of speech, writing, or thought that holds together clearly and makes sense.
Powerfully persuasive or interesting; strong enough to demand attention or belief.
Expressing ideas clearly in a few words, without unnecessary detail or filler.
In agreement or harmony with something; consistent with a set of ideas, values, or facts.
To draw out a response, feeling, or piece of information from someone, often by careful questioning or skilled communication.
The art of using language effectively and persuasively, especially in speaking or writing.
Clearly and briefly expressed, with nothing wasted; saying exactly what needs to be said and no more.
Very brief in speech or writing, to the point of seeming unfriendly, impatient, or dismissive.
An indirect reference to a person, event, or work that the speaker expects the audience to recognize, without naming it outright.
A comparison between two things that are different in most ways but share one key similarity, used to make an idea easier to understand.
A short, informal account of a real or supposedly real incident, often used to illustrate a point or entertain.
So ordinary and overused that it has lost any interest or originality; utterly predictable.
Characteristic of everyday spoken language rather than formal writing; informal in style.
To wander away from the main topic of a speech or piece of writing, often at length and without warning.
Not directly related to or necessary for the subject being discussed; coming from outside and adding nothing useful.
Using words in a non-literal way — through metaphor, simile, or other images — to suggest meaning beyond the plain sense.
A subtle difference in meaning, tone, or feeling that is easy to miss but important to a full understanding.
Lacking imagination or excitement; dull and unimaginative in a flat, uninspired way.
Not immediately obvious; working through small, careful signals rather than direct or heavy-handed expression.
Only loosely or indirectly connected to the main point; touching on a subject without engaging it directly.
A phrase or idea that was once fresh but has been used so many times it now sounds empty and unthinking.
Intended to teach a moral lesson, often in an overly instructive or moralising manner.
To improve someone's mind, character, or understanding, especially through instruction with a moral dimension.
To strongly urge or appeal to someone to do something, often with passion and a sense of moral urgency.
So overused or commonplace that it has lost all meaning or power; describing language or ideas worn out by repetition.
A talk or piece of writing that offers moral guidance, often at length and with more preaching than practical insight.
Lacking any strong, interesting, or memorable quality; dull and weak in a way that fails to engage or stimulate.
A dull, obvious moral statement offered as though it were a meaningful insight, especially one meant to comfort or advise.
Straightforward and matter-of-fact to the point of being dull; lacking imagination or poetic quality.
To say or do something again, often more than once, in order to make sure it is understood or remembered.
Excessively sweet, sentimental, or cheerful in a way that feels false or cloying rather than genuine.
More than what is needed or useful; present in excess so that it adds nothing and may even get in the way.
To spend too much time explaining or repeating something that is already understood, to the point of becoming tedious.
A leader who gains power by appealing to people's fears and prejudices rather than to reason, often using emotional speech to turn crowds against a particular group.
To express strong disapproval of something; to speak of something as having little value or as being wrong.
To call something into doubt or attack it as false or dishonest, especially someone's character, motives, or a stated fact.
To make someone extremely angry; to fill a person or group with outrage.
To cause something—usually a conflict, reaction, or harmful action—to begin, often by deliberately stirring people up.
To prove that a claim, argument, or person is wrong by using clear evidence or solid reasoning.
To protest or argue against something firmly; to make a formal objection or plea to someone in authority.
To firmly reject or refuse to accept something—a claim, an accusation, an idea, or an association—often in a public and forceful way.
A long, angry speech that criticizes someone or something harshly and at length, often losing control in the process.
Willing to listen, cooperate, or be guided; open to a suggestion or request without resistance.
To calm someone who is angry or upset by giving them what they want or by making a concession.
To make a painful feeling, fear, or worry less intense; to bring relief to distress or hunger.
Intended to reduce anger or hostility and bring about goodwill; showing a willingness to meet someone halfway.
